raw_evidence.label: The Economist's tourism-flow proxy for early COVID exposure
raw_evidence.content: On 6 March 2020, The Economist's Graphic Detail published 'Tracking the stealthy killer', arguing that the official COVID-19 case counts in many countries were implausibly low given how many travellers from China those countries had recently received. The piece used Chinese tour-group data through Q3 2019 as a proxy for total tourism flows between China and each country. By regressing logged confirmed cases on logged tourism (in OECD countries only, where surveillance was strongest), the piece produced an expected-cases curve. Countries lying far below the line — chiefly Indonesia, India, Russia and several other middle-income states — were flagged as likely under-reporting. The story landed at a sensitive moment: this was three days before Italy's national lockdown and five days before the WHO declared a pandemic, and it was one of the first English-language pieces to publicly argue that the rest of the world was already further into the outbreak than its case totals admitted.

raw_evidence.label: Johns Hopkins case data: 4 March 2020 snapshot
raw_evidence.content: Confirmed cases are the John Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 dashboard reading for 4 March 2020 — three days before publication. On that day the global confirmed total was approximately 95,000, dominated by Hubei province (67,332 cases) with major outbreaks in South Korea (5,621), Italy (3,089) and Iran (2,922). Most of the rest of the world reported only single- or double-digit case counts. The dashboard, run by Lauren Gardner's lab at JHU and described in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, became the de-facto global ledger of COVID-19 cases through 2020-2022. Its early-March snapshot is the snapshot of an outbreak that had spread far beyond Wuhan but was still being detected unevenly: the South Korean and Italian numbers were rising because those countries were testing aggressively, while many other nations had reported only a handful of imported cases despite extensive travel from affected regions.

raw_evidence.label: Global case landscape, 4 March 2020
raw_evidence.content: On 4 March 2020 the Johns Hopkins dashboard counted 95,124 confirmed COVID-19 cases worldwide. Mainland China alone held 80,271 of them — 84.4% of the global total. Hubei province by itself accounted for 67,332 cases (70.8% of global). Outside China only three countries had more than two thousand cases: South Korea (5,621), Italy (3,089) and Iran (2,922). The next group — Japan, France, Germany, Spain, the United States — sat between 150 and 350 cases each. Eighty-six countries had reported any cases at all; the remaining 55 in this dataset had reported zero.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_01 ===")
print(f"Total reported confirmed cases: {country_total.sum():,}")
print(f"Number of countries/regions reporting cases: {(country_total > 0).sum()}")
print(f"\nTop 15 by confirmed cases:")
for country, cases in country_total.head(15).items():
    pct = cases / country_total.sum() * 100
    print(f"  {country:25s} {int(cases):>7,}  ({pct:5.2f}%)")

china_total = country_total.get('China', 0)
print(f"\nChina (Mainland) share of global total: {china_total/country_total.sum()*100:.1f}%")

hubei = jh[jh['Province/State'] == 'Hubei']['Confirmed'].sum()
print(f"Hubei province alone: {int(hubei):,}  ({hubei/country_total.sum()*100:.1f}% of global)")

# Top 5 outside China
outside = country_total[country_total.index != 'China'].head(5)
print(f"\nTop 5 outside China:")
for c, v in outside.items():
    print(f"  {c:25s} {int(v):>7,}")

Source: Ministry of Culture and Tourism of the People's Republic of China — Q3 2019 outbound/inbound tourism statistics (http://zwgk.mct.gov.cn/auto255/202001/t20200102_850061.html) Facts: China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism publishes quarterly outbound and inbound tour-group counts for the top 30 destination/sender countries and continent residuals.; Q3 2019 was the most recent quarter available when The Economist's piece went to press in early March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Chinese tour-group data: the only consistent global tourism proxy in early 2020
raw_evidence.content: The exposure variable is unusual: it is not flight passenger counts, not tourist nights, not airline seats — it is Q3 2019 Chinese tour-group flows reported by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism. That ministry tracks group travellers to and from China for the top 30 sender/recipient countries plus continent residuals. The Economist used these because they covered both directions, broke out by destination country, and were the most recent globally consistent figures available — Q3 2019, six months before the analysis. They are an imperfect proxy because not all tourists travel in groups and they pre-date the outbreak itself, but for an early-March 2020 analysis they were the best harmonised cross-country exposure metric. The data are scaled in thousands of group-tourists per quarter; OECD countries like Japan (~3.6m) and South Korea (~2.7m) sit at the top, while many African and Latin American economies sit near zero.

Q3 2019 was the most recent quarter available when The Economist's piece went to press in early March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Tourism flows: where Chinese tour groups go
raw_evidence.content: Chinese outbound and inbound tour-group flows in Q3 2019 totalled about 8.94 million person-trips across these 124 countries. The flow is heavily concentrated: the top ten destinations account for 74.1% of the total. Thailand sits at the top with 1.55 million (almost twice Japan's 1.25 million); Taiwan, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia and Russia each saw 400,000 to 950,000 group-trips. OECD countries account for only 35% of total flow because the top non-OECD destinations — Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Russia — outweigh most OECD members. This concentration matters: it means a small number of non-OECD countries had the largest exposure but also some of the lowest reported case counts.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_03 ===")
mean_tour = (cov['outbound_tour_groups_Q3_2019_improved'] +
             cov['inbound_tour_groups_Q3_2019_1_improved']) / 2
cov['mean_tour'] = mean_tour
top_tour = cov.sort_values('mean_tour', ascending=False).head(15)
print("Top 15 countries by mean Chinese tour-group flows (Q3 2019):")
for _, row in top_tour.iterrows():
    flag = "OECD" if row['oecd'] else "    "
    print(f"  {flag}  {row['country']:25s}  {int(row['mean_tour']):>10,}")
print(f"\nTotal mean flow across all 124 countries: {int(mean_tour.sum()):,}")
print(f"OECD share of total flow: {(cov[cov.oecd==True]['mean_tour'].sum() / mean_tour.sum() * 100):.1f}%")
print(f"Top 10 share of total flow: {(top_tour.head(10)['mean_tour'].sum() / mean_tour.sum() * 100):.1f}%")

sentences.summary: det_05: Why tour groups predict outbreak size — and why the prediction has limits. Source: The Lancet — COVID-19 and Italy: what next? (https://www.thelancet.com/article/S0140-6736(20)30627-9/fulltext) Facts: Italy reported sustained community transmission from late February 2020 onward.; Italian authorities ordered national-level lockdown measures by 9 March 2020. | det_06: OECD vs non-OECD: surveillance capacity matters. Source: OECD — COVID-19 country responses (https://www.oecd.org/coronavirus/en/) Facts: The OECD comprises 34 high-income member countries (in 2020, before the 2020-2021 accessions).; OECD members had broadly comparable health-system testing infrastructure in early 2020 relative to non-OECD economies.

raw_evidence.label: Why tour groups predict outbreak size — and why the prediction has limits
raw_evidence.content: The mechanism the model assumes is direct seeding: people moving between countries carry the virus with them, and the more people, the more seeding events, the more confirmed cases (under symmetric surveillance). Empirically this is consistent with the early outbreak chronology — Italy, South Korea and Iran all had sustained transmission by late February, and all were major Chinese tour-group destinations or sources. But the model has real limits. (1) It uses only OECD countries to fit because OECD surveillance was assumed to be more uniform; non-OECD countries are then evaluated against this OECD-fit line, an extrapolation that may not hold. (2) Q3 2019 tourism is a proxy, not a measurement of who travelled in January-February 2020 specifically. (3) The single-variable model controls for nothing — temperature, healthcare capacity, age structure all matter and are absent. The Economist tested random forests, zero-inflated negative binomials and per-capita variants and reports that results were 'largely similar', but the simple OLS was kept for interpretability.

sources.title: The Lancet — COVID-19 and Italy: what next?
facts: Italy reported sustained community transmission from late February 2020 onward.
Italian authorities ordered national-level lockdown measures by 9 March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: OECD vs non-OECD: surveillance capacity matters
raw_evidence.content: The model is fit only on the 34 OECD countries in the dataset, then used to predict expected cases for the remaining ~90 countries. The premise is that OECD members had relatively comparable testing capacity in early March 2020, so an OECD-only fit captures the 'true' tourism-to-cases relationship without being polluted by countries that were simply not testing. Non-OECD residuals then inherit a specific interpretation: a country far below the OECD-fit line is not necessarily less infected, it is more likely to be less detected. Indonesia (population ~270m), India (~1.4bn) and Russia (~144m) are the headline cases — all populous, all with substantial pre-pandemic Chinese tourism, and all reporting case numbers in early March 2020 that were two to three orders of magnitude below what the OECD pattern predicted.

raw_evidence.label: OECD-only regression: log-tourism explains 59% of log-cases
raw_evidence.content: Fitting a simple linear regression on the 34 OECD countries gives log(cases+1) = -8.44 + 1.13 * log(mean tour-group flow). The slope is 1.13 (SE 0.17, t = 6.83, p < 1e-7) and the model explains R-squared = 0.59 of the variance in log-cases. The slightly super-linear slope means cases grow a little faster than tourism — doubling tourism predicts roughly a 2.2x increase in cases. The fit is strong enough to score every country against it: a country sitting on the line reports the cases its tourism flow would predict; a country far below is reporting fewer than expected; a country far above is reporting more.
raw_evidence.code:
oecd = pred[pred['oecd'] == True].copy()
non_oecd = pred[pred['oecd'] == False].copy()
print(f"OECD countries in fit: {len(oecd)}")
print(f"Non-OECD countries (held out / scored only): {len(non_oecd)}")

X = sm.add_constant(oecd['LogTourists'])
y = oecd['LogCases']
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary().as_text())

intercept, slope = model.params['const'], model.params['LogTourists']
r2 = model.rsquared
n = int(model.nobs)
p = model.f_pvalue
print(f"\nIntercept: {intercept:.4f}")
print(f"Slope (LogTourists coef): {slope:.4f}")
print(f"R-squared: {r2:.4f}")

raw_evidence.content: The mechanism the model assumes is direct seeding: people moving between countries carry the virus with them, and the more people, the more seeding events, the more confirmed cases (under symmetric surveillance). Empirically this is consistent with the early outbreak chronology — Italy, South Korea and Iran all had sustained transmission by late February, and all were major Chinese tour-group destinations or sources. But the model has real limits. (1) It uses only OECD countries to fit because OECD surveillance was assumed to be more uniform; non-OECD countries are then evaluated against this OECD-fit line, an extrapolation that may not hold. (2) Q3 2019 tourism is a proxy, not a measurement of who travelled in January-February 2020 specifically. (3) The single-variable model controls for nothing — temperature, healthcare capacity, age structure all matter and are absent. The Economist tested random forests, zero-inflated negative binomials and per-capita variants and reports that results were 'largely similar', but the simple OLS was kept for interpretability.

raw_evidence.label: OECD vs non-OECD: surveillance capacity matters
raw_evidence.content: The model is fit only on the 34 OECD countries in the dataset, then used to predict expected cases for the remaining ~90 countries. The premise is that OECD members had relatively comparable testing capacity in early March 2020, so an OECD-only fit captures the 'true' tourism-to-cases relationship without being polluted by countries that were simply not testing. raw_evidence.label: OECD-only regression: log-tourism explains 59% of log-cases
raw_evidence.content: Fitting a simple linear regression on the 34 OECD countries gives log(cases+1) = -8.44 + 1.13 * log(mean tour-group flow). The slope is 1.13 (SE 0.17, t = 6.83, p < 1e-7) and the model explains R-squared = 0.59 of the variance in log-cases. The slightly super-linear slope means cases grow a little faster than tourism — doubling tourism predicts roughly a 2.2x increase in cases. The fit is strong enough to score every country against it: a country sitting on the line reports the cases its tourism flow would predict; a country far below is reporting fewer than expected; a country far above is reporting more.

sentences.summary: det_07: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal. Source: Djalante et al. (2020) — Review and analysis of current responses to COVID-19 in Indonesia: Period of January to March 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7149002/) Facts: Indonesia reported 27 confirmed COVID-19 cases as of 11 March 2020.; Limited testing capacity meant Indonesia's true case count was almost certainly far higher than the official figure.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. In retrospect this was one of the earliest popular-press arguments that surveillance gaps, not absence of virus, explained the apparent geographic patchiness of the early pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. In retrospect this was one of the earliest popular-press arguments that surveillance gaps, not absence of virus, explained the apparent geographic patchiness of the early pandemic.

facts: Indonesia reported 27 confirmed COVID-19 cases as of 11 March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Most under-detected countries vs the OECD-fit prediction

raw_evidence.label: Full scatter: tourism flow vs reported cases
raw_evidence.content: Plotting all 124 countries in log-log space (mean Chinese tour-group flow on x, reported cases on y, with the OECD-only OLS line overlaid) gives the entire picture in one frame. The OECD points cluster around the line; non-OECD points scatter widely with most below it. Iran, Italy and South Korea sit far above. Russia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Myanmar sit conspicuously below. The fit is the spine of the entire piece: the line is a 'what should be there' baseline, and every country's distance from it tells a story about either their outbreak or their surveillance.

raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. facts: Indonesia reported 27 confirmed COVID-19 cases as of 11 March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Most under-detected countries vs the OECD-fit prediction

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. In retrospect this was one of the earliest popular-press arguments that surveillance gaps, not absence of virus, explained the apparent geographic patchiness of the early pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: Most under-detected countries vs the OECD-fit prediction
raw_evidence.content: Five countries sit more than 3.9 log-units below the OECD-fit line — the equivalent of reporting roughly 50 to 170 times fewer cases than the model expects. sentences.context: 05 · The other end
sentences.summary: det_04: Independent confirmation: COVID was massively under-reported in March 2020. Source: Lau et al. (2020) — Evaluating the massive underreporting and undertesting of COVID-19 cases in multiple global epicenters, Pulmonology (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7275155/) Facts: Mid-March 2020 fold-change under-reporting estimates: Iran 33.8x, France 46x, USA 53.8x, Italy 73x, Spain 161x.; The authors used the case-fatality ratio anomaly to back out an implied true infection count. Source: Li et al. (2020) — Substantial undocumented infection facilitates the rapid dissemination of novel coronavirus, Science (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aba9757) Facts: Modelling of pre-23-January 2020 outbreak in China estimated 86% of infections went undocumented.; Undocumented carriers were estimated to be the source of about 79% of documented cases.

raw_evidence.label: Independent confirmation: COVID was massively under-reported in March 2020
raw_evidence.content: Subsequent peer-reviewed research validated the Economist's hunch dramatically. A widely cited Pulmonology paper estimated 'fold change' under-reporting factors using case-fatality ratios as of mid-March 2020: Iran ~33.8x, France ~46x, the United States ~53.8x, Italy ~73x and Spain ~161x — meaning Spain's true caseload was on the order of 160 times its reported total. A Science paper estimated that 86% of all infections in China before 23 January 2020 were undocumented. Wuhan antibody surveys later suggested the true infection count there was nearly 10x the official tally. The Economist's piece came out before any of this seroprevalence work was possible, but its core claim — that the tourism-implied caseloads were enormously higher than the reported ones — was correct in direction and roughly right in magnitude.

sentences.summary: det_06: OECD vs non-OECD: surveillance capacity matters. Source: OECD — COVID-19 country responses (https://www.oecd.org/coronavirus/en/) Facts: The OECD comprises 34 high-income member countries (in 2020, before the 2020-2021 accessions).; OECD members had broadly comparable health-system testing infrastructure in early 2020 relative to non-OECD economies.

raw_evidence.label: OECD vs non-OECD: surveillance capacity matters
raw_evidence.content: The model is fit only on the 34 OECD countries in the dataset, then used to predict expected cases for the remaining ~90 countries. The premise is that OECD members had relatively comparable testing capacity in early March 2020, so an OECD-only fit captures the 'true' tourism-to-cases relationship without being polluted by countries that were simply not testing. Non-OECD residuals then inherit a specific interpretation: a country far below the OECD-fit line is not necessarily less infected, it is more likely to be less detected. Indonesia (population ~270m), India (~1.4bn) and Russia (~144m) are the headline cases — all populous, all with substantial pre-pandemic Chinese tourism, and all reporting case numbers in early March 2020 that were two to three orders of magnitude below what the OECD pattern predicted.

raw_evidence.label: OECD vs non-OECD: a systematic surveillance gap
raw_evidence.content: The OECD-only fit is mean-zero by construction, but the 90 non-OECD countries it was applied to are systematically below the line. Their mean residual is -0.85 log-units; their median is -0.73. Translated out of log space, non-OECD countries report on average about 43% of the cases the OECD-fit line would predict. 64% of non-OECD countries sit below the line, vs 56% of OECD members — a small gap in count, a large gap in size (the non-OECD residual SD is 1.69 vs 1.37 for OECD). The asymmetry is exactly what The Economist's argument predicts: cases per tourist look comparable in well-resourced systems and systematically smaller in less-resourced ones.

OECD members had broadly comparable health-system testing infrastructure in early 2020 relative to non-OECD economies.

raw_evidence.label: OECD vs non-OECD: a systematic surveillance gap
raw_evidence.content: The OECD-only fit is mean-zero by construction, but the 90 non-OECD countries it was applied to are systematically below the line. Their mean residual is -0.85 log-units; their median is -0.73. Translated out of log space, non-OECD countries report on average about 43% of the cases the OECD-fit line would predict. 64% of non-OECD countries sit below the line, vs 56% of OECD members — a small gap in count, a large gap in size (the non-OECD residual SD is 1.69 vs 1.37 for OECD). The asymmetry is exactly what The Economist's argument predicts: cases per tourist look comparable in well-resourced systems and systematically smaller in less-resourced ones.

print(f"  Mean residual (log): {oecd_resid.mean():+.3f}")
print(f"  Median residual:     {oecd_resid.median():+.3f}")
print(f"  SD:                  {oecd_resid.std():.3f}")
print(f"Non-OECD countries (n={len(non_resid)}):")
print(f"  Mean residual (log): {non_resid.mean():+.3f}")
print(f"  Median residual:     {non_resid.median():+.3f}")
print(f"  SD:                  {non_resid.std():.3f}")
print(f"\nDifference (non-OECD mean - OECD mean): {non_resid.mean() - oecd_resid.mean():+.3f} log-units")
print(f"Translated: non-OECD countries report on average exp({non_resid.mean() - oecd_resid.mean():.2f}) = {np.exp(non_resid.mean() - oecd_resid.mean()):.2f}x the OECD level relative to prediction.")

# Count by sign

print(f"OECD countries below their own line: {(oecd_resid < 0).sum()} of {len(oecd_resid)} ({(oecd_resid<0).mean()*100:.0f}%)")

raw_evidence.label: Full scatter: tourism flow vs reported cases
raw_evidence.content: Plotting all 124 countries in log-log space (mean Chinese tour-group flow on x, reported cases on y, with the OECD-only OLS line overlaid) gives the entire picture in one frame. The OECD points cluster around the line; non-OECD points scatter widely with most below it. Iran, Italy and South Korea sit far above. The fit is the spine of the entire piece: the line is a 'what should be there' baseline, and every country's distance from it tells a story about either their outbreak or their surveillance.

raw_evidence.label: OECD vs non-OECD: surveillance capacity matters
raw_evidence.content: The model is fit only on the 34 OECD countries in the dataset, then used to predict expected cases for the remaining ~90 countries. The premise is that OECD members had relatively comparable testing capacity in early March 2020, so an OECD-only fit captures the 'true' tourism-to-cases relationship without being polluted by countries that were simply not testing. Non-OECD residuals then inherit a specific interpretation: a country far below the OECD-fit line is not necessarily less infected, it is more likely to be less detected. Indonesia (population ~270m), India (~1.4bn) and Russia (~144m) are the headline cases — all populous, all with substantial pre-pandemic Chinese tourism, and all reporting case numbers in early March 2020 that were two to three orders of magnitude below what the OECD pattern predicted.

raw_evidence.label: Independent confirmation: COVID was massively under-reported in March 2020
raw_evidence.content: Subsequent peer-reviewed research validated the Economist's hunch dramatically. A widely cited Pulmonology paper estimated 'fold change' under-reporting factors using case-fatality ratios as of mid-March 2020: Iran ~33.8x, France ~46x, the United States ~53.8x, Italy ~73x and Spain ~161x — meaning Spain's true caseload was on the order of 160 times its reported total. A Science paper estimated that 86% of all infections in China before 23 January 2020 were undocumented. Wuhan antibody surveys later suggested the true infection count there was nearly 10x the official tally. The Economist's piece came out before any of this seroprevalence work was possible, but its core claim — that the tourism-implied caseloads were enormously higher than the reported ones — was correct in direction and roughly right in magnitude.

sources.title: Li et al. (2020) — Substantial undocumented infection facilitates the rapid dissemination of novel coronavirus, Science
facts: Modelling of pre-23-January 2020 outbreak in China estimated 86% of infections went undocumented.
Undocumented carriers were estimated to be the source of about 79% of documented cases.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. In retrospect this was one of the earliest popular-press arguments that surveillance gaps, not absence of virus, explained the apparent geographic patchiness of the early pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: Hidden-cases multiplier for the largest under-detectors
raw_evidence.content: Among countries whose model-predicted caseload is at least 50, twelve report dramatically less than expected. Russia (172x), Indonesia (165x), Myanmar (110x), Philippines (69x), Vietnam (54x), Thailand (51x), Taiwan (30x), New Zealand (27x), Malaysia (11x), Japan (5x), Singapore (5x) and Australia (3x). Read literally, these are the multipliers The Economist's model implies between true exposure and reported cases. Some of these countries — Singapore, Taiwan, Australia — may simply have effective testing-and-tracing programmes that prevented imported cases from blowing up. Others — Russia, Indonesia, Myanmar — fit a different, darker pattern: low testing, low reporting, large unseen outbreaks.

raw_evidence.content: Subsequent peer-reviewed research validated the Economist's hunch dramatically. facts: Indonesia reported 27 confirmed COVID-19 cases as of 11 March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Hidden-cases multiplier for the largest under-detectors
raw_evidence.content: Among countries whose model-predicted caseload is at least 50, twelve report dramatically less than expected. Russia (172x), Indonesia (165x), Myanmar (110x), Philippines (69x), Vietnam (54x), Thailand (51x), Taiwan (30x), New Zealand (27x), Malaysia (11x), Japan (5x), Singapore (5x) and Australia (3x). Read literally, these are the multipliers The Economist's model implies between true exposure and reported cases. Some of these countries — Singapore, Taiwan, Australia — may simply have effective testing-and-tracing programmes that prevented imported cases from blowing up. Others — Russia, Indonesia, Myanmar — fit a different, darker pattern: low testing, low reporting, large unseen outbreaks.
raw_evidence.output:
Top 12 under-detectors with multiplier:
Russia 172.5x; Indonesia 165.0x; Myanmar 109.9x; Philippines 69.2x; Vietnam 53.9x; Thailand 50.7x; Taiwan 29.7x; New Zealand 26.6x; Malaysia 11.1x; Japan 5.2x; Singapore 5.1x; Australia 3.1x

raw_evidence.label: Full scatter: tourism flow vs reported cases
raw_evidence.content: Plotting all 124 countries in log-log space (mean Chinese tour-group flow on x, reported cases on y, with the OECD-only OLS line overlaid) gives the entire picture in one frame. The OECD points cluster around the line; non-OECD points scatter widely with most below it. Iran, Italy and South Korea sit far above. Russia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Myanmar sit conspicuously below. The fit is the spine of the entire piece: the line is a 'what should be there' baseline, and every country's distance from it tells a story about either their outbreak or their surveillance.

raw_evidence.label: Independent confirmation: COVID was massively under-reported in March 2020
raw_evidence.content: Subsequent peer-reviewed research validated the Economist's hunch dramatically. A widely cited Pulmonology paper estimated 'fold change' under-reporting factors using case-fatality ratios as of mid-March 2020: Iran ~33.8x, France ~46x, the United States ~53.8x, Italy ~73x and Spain ~161x — meaning Spain's true caseload was on the order of 160 times its reported total. A Science paper estimated that 86% of all infections in China before 23 January 2020 were undocumented. Wuhan antibody surveys later suggested the true infection count there was nearly 10x the official tally. The Economist's piece came out before any of this seroprevalence work was possible, but its core claim — that the tourism-implied caseloads were enormously higher than the reported ones — was correct in direction and roughly right in magnitude.

sources.title: Li et al. (2020) — Substantial undocumented infection facilitates the rapid dissemination of novel coronavirus, Science
facts: Modelling of pre-23-January 2020 outbreak in China estimated 86% of infections went undocumented.
Undocumented carriers were estimated to be the source of about 79% of documented cases.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. In retrospect this was one of the earliest popular-press arguments that surveillance gaps, not absence of virus, explained the apparent geographic patchiness of the early pandemic.

raw_evidence.label: Independent confirmation: COVID was massively under-reported in March 2020
raw_evidence.content: Subsequent peer-reviewed research validated the Economist's hunch dramatically. A widely cited Pulmonology paper estimated 'fold change' under-reporting factors using case-fatality ratios as of mid-March 2020: Iran ~33.8x, France ~46x, the United States ~53.8x, Italy ~73x and Spain ~161x — meaning Spain's true caseload was on the order of 160 times its reported total. A Science paper estimated that 86% of all infections in China before 23 January 2020 were undocumented. Wuhan antibody surveys later suggested the true infection count there was nearly 10x the official tally. raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. raw_evidence.label: Why tour groups predict outbreak size — and why the prediction has limits
raw_evidence.content: The mechanism the model assumes is direct seeding: people moving between countries carry the virus with them, and the more people, the more seeding events, the more confirmed cases (under symmetric surveillance). Empirically this is consistent with the early outbreak chronology — Italy, South Korea and Iran all had sustained transmission by late February, and all were major Chinese tour-group destinations or sources. But the model has real limits. (1) It uses only OECD countries to fit because OECD surveillance was assumed to be more uniform; non-OECD countries are then evaluated against this OECD-fit line, an extrapolation that may not hold. (2) Q3 2019 tourism is a proxy, not a measurement of who travelled in January-February 2020 specifically. (3) The single-variable model controls for nothing — temperature, healthcare capacity, age structure all matter and are absent. The Economist tested random forests, zero-inflated negative binomials and per-capita variants and reports that results were 'largely similar', but the simple OLS was kept for interpretability.

raw_evidence.label: Why tour groups predict outbreak size — and why the prediction has limits
raw_evidence.content: The mechanism the model assumes is direct seeding: people moving between countries carry the virus with them, and the more people, the more seeding events, the more confirmed cases (under symmetric surveillance). Empirically this is consistent with the early outbreak chronology — Italy, South Korea and Iran all had sustained transmission by late February, and all were major Chinese tour-group destinations or sources. But the model has real limits. (1) It uses only OECD countries to fit because OECD surveillance was assumed to be more uniform; non-OECD countries are then evaluated against this OECD-fit line, an extrapolation that may not hold. (2) Q3 2019 tourism is a proxy, not a measurement of who travelled in January-February 2020 specifically. (3) The single-variable model controls for nothing — temperature, healthcare capacity, age structure all matter and are absent. The Economist tested random forests, zero-inflated negative binomials and per-capita variants and reports that results were 'largely similar', but the simple OLS was kept for interpretability.

sources.title: The Lancet — COVID-19 and Italy: what next?
facts: Italy reported sustained community transmission from late February 2020 onward.
Italian authorities ordered national-level lockdown measures by 9 March 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters: the cost of a missed early signal
raw_evidence.content: If the Economist's residuals were right, several countries were already weeks ahead of where their official numbers placed them — meaning their public-health responses were calibrated to the wrong outbreak size. Indonesia did not report community transmission until early March 2020 and was reporting fewer than 30 cases when the article ran; by April it was the country with the highest reported COVID-19 deaths in Southeast Asia. Iran's underreported caseload meant that hospitals were overwhelmed before officials acknowledged the scale of the outbreak. The Economist's argument was specifically that residual size could serve as an early-warning index: a country far below its tourism-implied prediction was not safe — it was probably blind. In retrospect this was one of the earliest popular-press arguments that surveillance gaps, not absence of virus, explained the apparent geographic patchiness of the early pandemic.
